results.title: [PDF] Outlier-Robust Multi-View Triangulation for Navigation
results.content: We apply Yang et al.’s (2020) Graduated Non-Convexity (GNC) algorithm to three chosen multi-view trian-gulation solvers and improve the best performing solver’s robustness to 50% outliers which outperforms the current state-of-the-art outlier removal method RANSAC. The first goal requires a comparison of the three current state-of-the-art multi-view triangulation solvers (AAT, Cifuentes and SVD) after the application of an outlier-robust technique (GNC) to assess their performance in outlier-dominated datasets. Figure 4-1 shows the performance of the three solvers (AAT, Cifuentes and SVD) without GNC implementation as a function of outlier rate for the three camera configurations (sphere, circle and line). 4.2 Goal 2: Applying the best combination to a lu-nar landing multi-view triangulation problem We have identified that TLS-Cifuentes is the best performing combination of outlier-robust method + solver. 49 Figure 4-5: Performance of Cifuentes and SVD Multi-view Triangulation Solvers with GNC-TLS on the parabolic camera configuration dataset. Additionally, this work’s implementation of GNC-TLS with the Cifuentes solver performed better than the current state-of-the-art outlier removal method for triangulation, RANSAC on all simulated camera configurations.

results.title: Regularized Covariance Estimation Guide - Number Analytics
results.content: Regularized covariance estimation has become an essential component in modern data analysis across diverse fields such as finance, genomics, and machine learning. In this article, we explore strategies for covariance matrix estimation using regularization techniques, aiming to provide insight into the theoretical foundations as well as practical implementation. ### Motivation for Regularization Traditional sample covariance estimators can be unstable, especially in high-dimensional settings where p≈n p \approx n p≈n or even p>n p > n p>n. Regularization methods help mitigate these issues by “shrinking” the covariance estimates towards more structured or parsimonious models, leading to improved out-of-sample performance and computational stability. ### Shrinkage Estimators Shrinkage estimators reduce the variance of the covariance matrix estimator by pulling the sample covariance matrix towards a “target” matrix. Regularized covariance estimation can be implemented in various programming languages. * We then estimate the covariance matrix with a shrinkage approach. Below is an example using the Ledoit-Wolf estimator: from sklearn.covariance import LedoitWolf import matplotlib.pyplot as plt cov_shrunk = lw.fit(data).covariance_ plt.imshow(cov_shrunk, cmap='viridis') plt.title('Shrunk Covariance Matrix') * Synthetic data is generated with 100 observations of 50 variables. * The `LedoitWolf` estimator is used to compute the regularized covariance matrix, and a heatmap is plotted for visualization. Regularized covariance estimators are often used in dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA) and in classification algorithms that rely on linear discriminant analysis (LDA) to enhance generalization performance, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional features 5. When implementing regularized covariance estimation, consider the following best practices: 1. * Consider the sensitivity of your covariance estimates to changes in data and parameter settings. Here’s an example of a Mermaid diagram that outlines the regularization process: This diagram summarizes the decision-making process when choosing between standard and regularized covariance estimation techniques depending on the data's dimensionality. Regularized covariance estimation is a powerful tool in modern multivariate analysis, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional datasets. Regularized estimation of large covariance matrices. A shrinkage approach to large-scale covariance matrix estimation and implications for functional genomics. Armed with both theoretical insight and practical code examples, you can now implement regularized covariance estimation techniques to improve stability, avoid overfitting, and foster robust multivariate analyses.

results.title: What is a solver & solver phases - Optimization Hub
results.content: A **solver** is a tool, algorithm, or program designed to find solutions to a specific type of problem, typically mathematical, logical, computational, or engineering in nature. **Optimization solvers (or mathematical solvers)**. •        Examples: Linear programming solvers like Gurobi, CPLEX, or open-source options like HIGHS and SCIP. •        Examples: SAT solvers (for Boolean satisfiability problems) or constraint programming tools like Google OR-Tools. In OR, by solver we mean either an optimization model with model & build + solve phases or a mathematical solver. **MATH EQUATIONS + MODEL BUILDER + MATHEMATICAL SOLVER = PROBLEM SPECIFIC SOLVER**. The model is sent to a mathematical solver for solving. Mathematical solvers are open-source (HiGHS, SCIP, GLOP, CP-SAT, CBC etc.) or commercial (Gurobi Optimization, CPLEX, Xpress, MOSEK ApS, COPT, Knitro, Hexaly etc). After modeling your problem in the programming language of your choice, you can use  commercial or open-source solvers to solve it. They call mathematical solvers which execute the solve phase.

results.title: Solvers — ASKAP Central Processor documentation
results.content: A number of solvers are available in ASKAPsoft. For imaging purposes only specialized image solvers are generally used, although generic SVD-based linear solver (see the diagram above) can be used with (very small) images as well (some change to the code may be required as this is not a normal use case). The *solver* parset parameter defines the type of the image solver to use with the choice between *Dirty*, *and Clean*. The *Dirty* solver just inverts the data (takes the normal equations and simply divides the data vector by the diagonal of the normal matrix. This is analogous to making the dirty image or a linear mosaic of dirty images), while the Clean performs minor cycle cleaning. The Restore solver is somewhat special. It is executed behind the scene with very minimal setup required from the user (the same parameters are generally used as for the cleaning solver). Restore solver is described separately in the cimager. Parameters **verbose** and **tolerance** have **solver.Clean** or **solver.Dirty** prefix. Although verbose is understood by dirty solver, there is currently no effect. **Dirty** solver doesn’t require any additional parameters (but one can also set up a preconditioner described in the following section with the dirty solver).
